sections.name: Client-Server Architecture
sections.explanation_simple: In multiplayer games, one computer (the server) is the 'source of truth' and everyone else (clients) connect to it. Think of it like a restaurant: the server is the kitchen that knows the real state of things (what food is actually ready), and clients are the waiters who tell the kitchen what you want and bring you updates. The server prevents cheating because it doesn't trust what clients say - it validates everything. This is why you can't just tell the server 'I have infinite health' - the server checks your actual health.
key_concepts: Server Authority: Server makes all final decisions (player position, health, game state)
Client: Runs your game, sends inputs to server, renders what server says
Dedicated Server: Server-only program with no graphics (used by big games)
Listen Server: One player's game also acts as server (peer-to-peer-ish)
Tick Rate: How many times per second the server updates (64 Hz typical)
Packet: A single chunk of data sent over network
Bandwidth: How much data can be sent per second
Latency: Time for data to travel (your ping)
Packet Loss: When packets don't arrive

sections.name: Lag Compensation Techniques
sections.explanation_simple: Lag compensation makes online games feel smooth even when players have high ping. Imagine you're playing on a server in New York, but your friend is in Australia with 300ms ping. Without lag compensation, your friend would see things happening 0.3 seconds late - everything would feel sluggish. There are three main tricks to fix this: 1) Client-side prediction - your game predicts what will happen before the server confirms it, 2) Entity interpolation - smooths out the jerky position updates into smooth movement, and 3) Rollback netcode (used in fighting games) - rewinds time to check if a punch actually landed.
key_concepts: Client-side Prediction: Client moves immediately, then corrects when server responds
Server Reconciliation: Client compares its state with server's authoritative state
Entity Interpolation: Smoothly moves other players between known positions
Extrapolation: Guessing where someone will be based on current velocity
Rollback Netcode: Saves past states, processes inputs, and corrects if wrong (used in Street Fighter 6, Guilty Gear)
Input Delay: Waiting a few frames before showing action (helps feel consistent)
Latency Hiding: Showing effects/animations immediately even if damage hasn't been confirmed

sections.name: Open World Streaming & Optimization
sections.explanation_simple: Open world games like GTA V, Skyrim, and Breath of the Wild have massive worlds that can't fit in memory all at once. The trick is streaming - only loading the parts of the world near the player. Imagine a book with thousands of pages - you don't carry the whole book in your hands, you just read the page you're on. When you turn the page, you load the next one. Open world games do the same thing with chunks of the world. UE5's World Partition system does this automatically.
key_concepts: World Partition: Divides map into grid cells, loads cells near player
Streaming: Loading/unloading assets as needed (not all at once)
LOD (Level of Detail): Far-away objects use simpler models
Chunk Loading: Standard 2D grid for dividing open worlds
Async Loading: Loading assets in background while game runs
Memory Budget: Maximum memory the game can use
Seamless World: No loading screens as you traverse (most impressive)
Fast Travel: Teleporting between discovered locations

sections.name: FPS & TPS Combat Systems
sections.explanation_simple: First-person and third-person shooter combat is the most popular game genre. At its core, it's about pointing a weapon and clicking. But the details make the difference between a great shooter (Call of Duty, Destiny, Apex Legends) and a clunky one. The big questions: Is it hitscan (instant hit, like a laser pointer) or projectile (bullet travels, like in real life)? How does recoil work (does the gun kick up, or does the spread randomize)? How does the game know if you hit something? These systems work together to make shooting feel satisfying.
key_concepts: Hitscan: Instant hit detection (bullet arrives the same frame you fire)
Projectile: Bullet with travel time and drop (used in Battlefield, PUBG)
ADS: Aim Down Sights (zooming in for accuracy)
Recoil: Gun moves upward as you fire (pattern or random)
Spread/Accuracy: Random deviation of bullets (hip fire is less accurate)
Raycast: Shooting a ray from camera to check what it hits
Headshot: Extra damage for hitting the head (critical hit)
Damage Falloff: Less damage over distance
FOV: Field of View (how much you can see)
Hip Fire: Shooting without aiming (less accurate but faster)
